key_insight: If a medical AI was trained on a patient’s past data, its predictions on that same patient’s future data can shift in biased ways — a phenomenon the authors call memorisation bias.
clinical_relevance: This matters because returning patients may receive less accurate diagnostic support: sensitivity can drop for new conditions, while apparent performance can be artificially inflated when their health status has not changed.
method: Compared predictions on patients’ future records with vs without their own historical data included in training
Tested the effect across multiple data modalities and model architectures
Simulated prospective deployment scenarios for returning contributors
evidence_signal: The abstract reports that memorisation bias persisted across diverse datasets, modalities, and models, sometimes affecting records acquired decades after the training data.
watch_item: De-identification can make it hard to detect or exclude returning contributors, so deployment systems may need safeguards to reduce patient-specific leakage from training data.
